Senses.Explanation: The command to take down the banner-pole at the gate. The records preserve the same turn: Mahakasyapa calls Ananda, Ananda responds, and Mahakasyapa orders him to lower the pole. The command, not a discursive explanation, closes the exchange. Later masters keep reopening that closure as a public case. An unnamed monk tells Buhui Fatong that this one saying concerns everyone's life, while Juelang Daosheng calls it a sentence that opens a lock yet remains difficult to pass through. Xiuye Minglin and Tian'an Sheng raise the inherited wording and then test or criticize how it is met. The Zen bend is therefore observable in its reuse: an architectural command becomes a quoted encounter, a test question, and an object of later capping and appraisal, while the corpus never licenses replacing the words with an outside symbolic equation.

Senses.Explanation: The four graphs are the body-idiom of total disclosure - pour out the belly, tip out the guts, hold nothing back in showing someone - and the corpus prices it across five registers: the case-verse promise with the addressee in the rhyme slot, from Dahui Zonggao, Songyuan Chongyue and Miyun Yuanwu - with the same Dahui verse standing again in the life of Nanquan in the 1183 lamp, and the different verse of Yuanri on the same case - the live answer-word that is itself the whole reply, in Chijue Daochong, Shixi Xinyue and Yulin Tongxiu; the figure-manner naming of how the old ones gave, in Wuchu Daguan, Wuwen Daocan and Wuhuan Xingchong; the critique that faults even total pouring-out, from Xueyan Zuqin; and the limit admission that pouring everything out still cannot exhaust, in Chisong Daoling. Born as a verse-promise. Dahui's verse on Nanquan's not-mind-not-buddha-not-thing address opens with the promise and the price: pour out belly and guts and tell you - why do you still hum and hold back? - then the charge: grab it hard this very now and hand it to the person without affairs. The verse circulated standing: the 1183 lamp carries it inside Nanquan's own life, naming him by his sobriquet, with the hum-and-now copy-variants against his own record's bytes; and a second master, Yuanri, opened a different verse on the same case - pour out belly and guts: how many know it? Not a hair to lean on. Songyuan Chongyue quotes Dahui's weeping-laughing verse on the Baizhang case, remarks that he still folds his hands behind the ancients' backs - then adds his own: weeping not-through, laughing not-through, pour out belly and guts and tell you; if father and son are not kin, do you know it or not? Lift your head - three pounds of iron behind the skull. Miyun Yuanwu's Ming case-verse on Dongshan's eighteen-year-old-daughter answer runs the same promise: pour out belly and guts and tell you - no need for doubt and further tangle. Yuelin Shiguan's titled verse on the transformation-one whose five viscera were stolen makes the thief the addressee: suddenly meeting the thief who takes in broad daylight, pour out belly and guts and hand it to him. Spent as the answer itself. Chijue Daochong's retelling of the Zaoshan Guangren case turns on it: when Zaoshan asks why the questioner keeps squeezing him - meal at mealtime, bed at night, why keep pressing me? - the presider's answer-turn is the block: pour out belly and guts and tell people. Shixi Xinyue's installation-day exchange: how is the last word? - pour out belly and guts toward whom? - and when pressed whether he got the line at Yunju or at Yunding, the answer floats free of both: a floating life's chiseling has nothing to do with it. Yulin Tongxiu's is the tersest form: the questioner asks the import of the World-Honored-One never having taken a life since the worthies' kalpa - the whole answer is the four graphs, and the bow draws the coda: rarely met, the guest who can take it in through the ear. Naming how the old figures gave. Wuchu Daguan's hall address pairs the case-figures in couplets - the immovable-wisdom one of awakened mind long in the seven-out-eight-in; the elder Gavampati facing people pouring out belly and guts - then the knee-slap and the closing line: folded cloud-mountains drawing the spirit long. Wuwen Daocan prices the telling by an image: the sweet melon sweet through the stem, the bitter gourd bitter at the root - pour out belly and guts and tell people, just like rain on the apricot-branch blossoms. Wuhuan Xingchong's eight-verse set on pointing at mind opens: the mouth throws out a whole piece of heart, where thought stirs no one knows the tone - the house-watching words a thousand years out: pour out belly and guts and tell you. Even pouring-out can fail, and it has a limit. Xueyan Zuqin's raised comment on Yunmen's coin-for-a-barley-cake address names the fault: the lame-footed master cherishing his beloved son - his every move is pouring out belly and guts - only he does it too hurriedly, with something sticky on the teeth; this humble seat does otherwise. And Chisong Daoling's memorial address for the governor who died for the dynasty names the limit: think of the late one exhausting loyal sincerity, forgetting life-and-death, repaying ruler and parent, taking benevolence and righteousness - this mountain-monk, arriving here, let him pour out belly and guts: words still cannot exhaust it. The pour never changes; what the record prices is whether it lands - the addressee humming, the rain on the blossoms, or the rarely-met ear.

Senses.Explanation: A precept is a binding rule that can be received, kept, broken, and enforced. The records do not flatten that rule into either automatic obedience or automatic rejection. Yongjue Yuanxian places two inherited sayings together: ‘the one word precept is what the buddhas take as teacher’ (戒之一字，諸佛所師) and ‘the one word precept is what the patriarchs avoid’ (戒之一字，諸祖所忌), then asks why buddhas and patriarchs appear to part ways. Zhuanyu Guanheng calls precept a name for guiding people and asks where it can be established when inner and outer distinctions are examined; he identifies its basis with what one originally is and says reception neither subtracts nor adds to it. Gaofeng Yuanmiao says Bodhidharma's line did not foreground receiving precepts, but adds that it never instructed anyone deliberately to destroy them and that no one transmitted the mind seal without observing precepts and discipline. The rule also enters public interview: when an unnamed monk asks Wufeng Ruxue ‘what is precept?’, Wufeng raises his whisk. Qianshan Shengren Hanke says mind and precept are not two, yet immediately warns those who have received precepts not to treat them lightly. Muchen Daomin says only a buddha keeps the pure precept and all others are breakers; Poshan Haiming says keeping does not send one to heaven and violation does not send one to hell, while still naming ‘true keeping.’ Chunbei Guangde calls the word uncommon, Meixi Fudu calls it the basis of becoming a buddha, and Muchen calls it the foundation on which stability and insight are built. These are attested tensions within one hard rule, not grounds for deleting it from the entry.

Senses.Explanation: Precepts and discipline join the binding rules to the code that orders them. Gaofeng Yuanmiao says that Bodhidharma's line did not foreground receiving precepts, yet no one transmitted the mind seal without observing precepts and discipline. Wuhuan Xingchong praises conduct that keeps them as strictly as frost. Dazhu Huihai uses the compound in the opposite direction, describing an awakened person as not constrained by precepts and discipline; that claim tests constraint rather than pretending the rules are absent. The lay preface writer Yan Dacan says that strict observers have become few while describing Jizong Che. Wuzhuo Wenxi tells the old man he meets that late-age monks seldom follow precepts and discipline, and Zhongfeng Mingben calls them the root of monastic ritual forms. The compound thus names a real regulatory structure whose relation to freedom is disputed inside the records.

The precepts are the articulated body of rules received and observed as precepts. Tianru Weize defines discipline as the precepts. Meixi Fudu asks what use the precepts have once the deluded activity for which they were established has ended. Juelang Daosheng answers an unnamed questioner who asks about the diamond-like precepts of one's own nature, while Mixing Jiren warns applicants not to treat the precepts as indirect. Yongjue Yuanxian asks whether they lie in the platform, purity, the ordination formula, teachers, conduct, robes, or begging, and refuses to reduce them to any one perishing form.
Senses.Note: Reception, instruction, and rule/code passages concern one body of precepts rather than different things. Headings that mean an address on the precepts segment as “precept address” and are not evidence for another sense.
